happens: Walking puts about 1.2× his weight on one leg at each step. The sim sets that against both legs’ 1.4× push (a rough rule: a near-straight leg is much stronger than one in a squat), and he has 35× what walking needs. Running uses the Sprint tab’s rough rule: strength above his weight. Real runners land with 2–2.9× their weight on one leg, on springy, near-straight legs the dial doesn’t model.His feet press 47.6 kPa into the concrete slab, which gives at about 2.5 MPa.
math: Volume = 0.1002 × height³ (his build, from his ruled mass at 1,060 kg/m³: 2.84 m³ at 10 ft) = 2.84 m³; mass = density × volume = 1,060 kg/m³ × 2.84 m³ = 3.01 t; weight W = m g = 29.5 kN. Both legs push up to 1.4 × strength = 1.25 MN. Stand: ≥ W. Walk: ≥ 1.2 W, the load on one leg per step (Nilsson & Thorstensson 1989), set against both legs’ push (a rough rule). Run (the Sprint tab’s rough rule): strength > W; measured running peaks are 2–2.9 W per step. Feet: W ÷ (2 × 0.31 m²) = 47.6 kPa. Whole underside: W ÷ 0.7 m² = 42.3 kPa. Sand and gravel: below the failure pressure his feet leave a print scaled from a weighed elephant’s (Schanz 2013: 18 mm at 350 kPa, rising as pressure^1.27 and with foot width). That elephant’s sand carried its forefoot (350 kPa by the researchers’ calibrated model; force-plate data suggest nearer 181 kPa) with only a 2 cm print, so we take 350 kPa as where it starts to fail, scaled with foot width, and more for gravel, which bears more (our estimate; if 181 kPa is right, sinking starts sooner). Past it the foot sinks until limit + γ·depth·N_q carries it (N_q 18.4 or 64.2; USACE EM 1110-1-1905). Clay: the bearing grows with depth (N_c up to 9; EM 1110-1-1905 Table 4-7) plus γ·depth. All estimates. Bedrock carries up to 1.7 GPa × his underside = 1.18 GN (estimate). Bolted to the planet stops sliding, not sinking; only Comic ground keeps the floor whole. Inside the Earth: PREM density and gravity (Dziewonski & Anderson 1981); resistance = area × (rock strength + ρv²) against his motion relative to the turning rock; no strength in the liquid outer core; 3-D RK4 for the first trip, Earth turning once per 23.93 h; later trips averaged. His gravity treats him as a ball of equal volume, radius 88 cm. Surface gravity GM/R², escape speed √(2GM/R), G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹. His pull equals the Earth’s at √(GM/g) = 0.14 mm. Air: Bondi radius GM/c² with c = 340 m/s = 1.7 × 10⁻⁹ mm; rate 4πλG²M²ρ/c³ with λ = 0.625 (rough, no heating feedback). Rock crushed where ρ_rock·GM/r tops 1.7 GPa: 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ mm (unconfined surface rock, 200 MPa: 2.7 × 10⁻⁹ mm). Gravitational drag on the rock he moves through: F = 4πG²m²ρ I(v/c_s)/v² (Ostriker 1999, written for a gas; I → M³/3 when slow, ln Λ = 5 when fast, an estimate). c_s = 6 km/s stands in for rock (an estimate; PREM wave speeds in solid rock run 3.2–13.7 km/s). The ranges use 3.2 km/s at the fast end and no gravitational drag at the slow end. Black hole when 2GM/c² ≥ R: density ≥ 3c²/(8πGR²) = 2.1 × 10²⁶ kg/m³ at this height.

happens: The ground held. On the concrete slab it gives at 1.55 MN of push.Real muscle caps his leg speed, so the jump tops out near 18.3 m/s of takeoff speed however strong he gets.He lands on bent legs and stops over the same 76 cm leg stroke he jumped with, so the ground takes 4.9× his weight for 200 ms (9.4% of what the concrete slab can bear).
math: Legs push his body (2,920 kg) up and his feet (87 kg) down with 480 kN at most (140% of the strength he uses, 343 kN: the legs also carry his body weight), falling with speed per the Hill curve over 0.76 m. Gravity holds the body back. The ground holds the feet with its bearing strength (1.55 MN for both feet) plus an inertial term ρv²A once they move. At full extension the legs lock: takeoff momentum = body momentum − feet momentum. Flight integrated with drag (Cd 1.0, 0.7 m² head-first); no-air height from energy conservation in Earth’s 1/r² gravity.

s1-collide.verdict: Rex doesn’t budge. Ollie stops dead against him, and the blow goes through his bolts into the planet.
status: Charge: 25.2 m/s (his sprint after a 28.7 m run-up)Bolted: Earth takes the blowRock cracks 24 cm around his boltsNo noticeable quake
tiles: Charge speed25.2 m/shis sprint after a 28.7 m run-upEnergy freed at the hit957 kJ230 g TNT · 1.9× a Corolla at 100 km/hRex movesnot at allboltedForce of the hit3.04 MNover 25 ms (plush squash, estimate)Earth’s speed change1.3 × 10⁻²⁰ m/sit would take 2.5 billion years to move 1 mm
effort: Effort: 20% of their strength (each as hard as lifting 18 t). The hardest both can go while nothing around them breaks.Courtesy ceiling: 20% (lifting 18 t). Past that, the hit’s air blast risks damage 5 m away.
happens: Momentum is never lost. Whatever Ollie brings in, the two of them (plus whatever holds Rex) carry away. A splat shares it and frees the rest of the energy as heat, sound and blast. A perfect bounce keeps all the energy as motion. Soft bodies sit near the splat end.“Immovable” only means what holds Rex in place. Bolted, he is part of the planet: the bolts hand the momentum to the Earth’s 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg.How hard they hit depends on how squishy they are, which nobody knows for an indestructible plush. If they squash by a quarter of the smaller body’s thickness (32 cm in all), the hit lasts 25 ms and pushes with about 3.04 MN. A perfectly rigid body would make the force infinite, but relativity forbids one: no push travels through a body faster than light. Even the stiffest body physics allows takes 2.1 ns to stop, which limits the average force to about 36.1 TN.The Earth takes the momentum: its speed changes by 1.3 × 10⁻²⁰ m/s. And Ollie got his speed by pushing on the Earth in the first place, so the Earth just gets its own momentum back and ends up exactly as still as it started.The bolts are comic; the rock isn’t. The load on the rock around his bolts is 3.04 MN: granite pulls apart within about 24 cm and is crushed within about 4.9 cm, and the concrete slab on top tears at 4.4× its limit.
callouts: A loud thump: the hit lasts 25 ms, too slow to make a blast wave, so the 230 g TNT goes into heating and squashing them.
math: Charge: his sprint after a 28.7 m run-up → v = 25.2 m/s; momentum p = γ m v = 75,900 kg·m/s. Splat: they move off as one body. Invariant mass M = √(m₁² + m₂² + 2m₂E₁/c²); energy freed Q = (M − m₁ − m₂)c² (½μv² below 1% of light speed, μ = m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂)). Perfect bounce: each body’s momentum reverses in the centre-of-momentum frame. Below 1% of light speed: v₁′ = (m₁−m₂)/(m₁+m₂)·v, v₂′ = 2m₁/(m₁+m₂)·v. Held: Rex and the Earth act as one body; Earth’s Δv = p/(m + M_Earth). Force: squash s = ½ × the smaller depth = 32 cm; F = Q/s (splat) or 2Q/s peak (bounce). Ordinary solids and liquids at everyday pressures can’t carry sound faster than about 36 km/s; nothing travels faster than light, which limits the average force. Run-up: m u du/dx = T − k u², so u = u_top √(1 − e^(−2kx/m)) over x = 28.7 m, capped by his legs. Slide: x = m/(2k)·ln(1 + kV²/R), k = ½ρ₀C_dA. Rock: a force C spread over a half-sphere of radius r averages C/(2πr²); granite pulls apart at 8.4 MPa and crushes at 200 MPa, so r = √(C/2πσ). Blast radii: Kinney & Graham (1985), as if all of Q became a blast (upper bound). Quake: 1 part in 10,000 of Q (the usual share, give or take ⅔ of a magnitude), as if all of Q reached the ground, which overstates it. Ollie’s horns don’t change the momentum or the energy; they only put the force on a smaller patch.

s3-wrestle-friction-friction.verdict: Pushing straight across: dead heat. Both are far stronger than their footing (each holds only 17.7 kN), so strength stops mattering. If they shoved instead, all-out (see Shove, where the courtesy ceiling keeps it gentle), they’d fly apart like skaters: Rex at 14.5 m/s, Ollie at 14.4 m/s.
status: Rex holds 17.7 kN · drives 17.7 kNOllie holds 17.7 kN · drives 17.7 kN
tiles: WinnernobodystalematePush between them17.7 kNthe same both ways
effort: All-out: no cap needed. Nothing the lab checks in this test can do harm here (nearest people and buildings 5 m away), so they go all-out.Courtesy ceiling: none. Nothing in this test does harm, even all-out, with the nearest people and buildings 5 m away.
happens: A shoving match is decided at the feet. To push forward, each one has to grip the ground; to stay put, each one has to grip it too. Strength past that grip just makes feet slide. (That assumes each leans into the push; upright, a body tips over at a few hundred newtons.)Walking drive is friction under his own weight (plus a little claw or boot bite if dug in): 17.7 kN for Rex, 17.7 kN for Ollie. Holding still can use his full footing.Equal bodies on equal ground stay equal at any strength. A heavier body, or one dug in, wins.
callouts: Each is strong enough to lift the other, so a real bout goes to whoever gets lower first and pushes upward, taking the weight off the other’s feet. The sim can’t model that.
math: Hold = min(strength, footing); footing = μ m g (+ shear × buried area if dug in; unlimited if bolted). Drive = min(strength, μ m g + ¼ shear × buried area if dug in); 0 if bolted or too heavy to walk. Winner: the one whose drive beats the other’s hold. Walk-out: a = (drive − hold) / (m_Rex + m_Ollie), capped at his running speed, over half the ring (3.47 m).

s4-catch.verdict: Rex lobs the baseball at 8.62 m/s. It reaches Ollie 1.22 s later at 8.32 m/s. It hits his waiting hands with 65.9 N to 165 N, and his arms bring it in over 91 cm. One round trip takes about 3.99 s (the throws and flights).

happens: The gentlest throw that gets there leaves at about 44°. With no air it would be 45° at 8.46 m/s; drag asks for 1.9% more.Catching is stopping momentum, and here most of it happens in the first instant. His hands wait at full reach, and with his forearms they weigh 132 kg, more than the baseball. When it hits them they move off together, and nearly all of its energy goes into squashing his palms and the baseball by about 3 cm to 7.6 cm (an estimate). That’s the 65.9 N to 165 N, and the catch itself is over in about 7.3 ms to 18 ms. Bringing it in to his chest (91 cm) takes as long as he likes: he has strength to spare, and the gentlest steady push that does it, 1.02 N, takes 3.34 min.The round trip counts the throws and the flights. With strength to spare, each catcher brings the baseball in to his chest as slowly as he likes, so that part has no set time.
Stopping it puts 5.95 J (1.4 mg TNT) into his palms and arms. It ends up as heat in his indestructible plush.
math: Aim: the gentlest throw is the angle needing the least launch speed, each speed solved so the arc comes down at Ollie’s hand height (2.74 m) where his hands meet it, 1.82 m in front of his centre. Same air and round-Earth model as Throw. Fastball: his full-strength speed at each angle; the flattest angle whose path passes Ollie’s hands. Catch: first contact with his hands (m_h = 132 kg): v₁ = v m/(m + m_h); energy lost ½ m m_h v²/(m + m_h), over a 3 cm–7.6 cm squash (1–2.5% of his height, an estimate). Then F = (m + m_h) v₁²/(2d) + m g sin(angle) if his feet hold (F ≤ R); otherwise F/(m + m_h) + (F − R_slide(F))/M = v_eff²/(2d) and he slides. d = 0.3 × his height = 91 cm. First contact lasts about 2 × squash / v. At the arm force F the stroke takes t = v₁/a, a = (F − m g sin(angle))/(m + m_h) (plus his own slide back); at the least force that works, t = 2d/v₁. The round trip counts that stroke only when it is forced (he slides or needs at least half his strength); otherwise he can take as long as he likes. Slide: the pair coasts to a stop against friction and air drag: x = (M+m)/(2k)·ln(1 + k u²/R).
